seo_title: Bunny Man: the 1970 Virginia sightings, explained
seo_desc: Two police reports from Burke, Virginia in October 1970, the hatchet and the porch post, and how Bunny Man Bridge collected fifty years of invented murders.
summary: A man in a rabbit suit with an axe, traced back to two police reports from Burke, Virginia in October 1970 and then buried under decades of made-up killings.
body: The Bunny Man is a northern Virginia legend about a figure in a rabbit costume who goes after people with an axe, usually at the Colchester Overpass near Clifton, which everybody now calls Bunny Man Bridge.

This one has a documented start, which is unusual. Fairfax County library historian-archivist Brian Conley traced it to two police reports from Burke in October 1970. A man in a bunny suit threw a hatchet through a car window in the first, and a man in a bunny costume chopped at a porch post and threatened a security guard in the second.
The rest is embellishment. The escaped inmate, the murders, the bodies under the bridge, none of it is in the police record, and by 1973 the story already had 54 versions.

p: Robert Bennett was a cadet at the US Air Force Academy, home in Burke visiting relatives with his fiancée. They were coming back from a football game and parked in a field on Guinea Road around midnight to walk over to an uncle's house across the road, engine still running.

Something moved outside the back window. A man in a white suit with long rabbit ears came out of the bushes shouting that they were on private property and that he had their tag number, then threw a hatchet through the passenger window and ran off. They got out of there and the hatchet was still on the floorboard when they reached the police.

There's a detail I like because it's how real reports read. Bennett said the man had long bunny ears. His fiancée said there were no ears, just a white pointed hood of some kind. Both of them got a clear look at his face and neither could tell his race in the dark. The police examined the hatchet, found nothing to work with and gave it back to Bennett, and that was the end of it.

On the evening of October 31, 1970, a construction security guard named Paul Phillips walked up to a man standing on the porch of an unfinished empty house in Kings Park West, off the same road. Phillips said he was wearing a grey, black and white bunny costume, looked about 20, and stood 5 ft 8 and about 175 lb.

Phillips started talking to him and the man started chopping at a porch post with a long-handled axe. Some accounts count eight gashes in the post. He told Phillips that all you people trespass around here, and that if Phillips came any closer he'd chop his head off.

Phillips went back to his car for his handgun. By the time he got back the rabbit was gone into the woods, and that was the last documented sighting of a man in a rabbit suit with an axe in that county.

sections.h: The month it became a story
p: When the Washington Post picked the story up, more than 50 people called police to say they'd seen the Bunny Man. One paper reported that he'd eaten somebody's runaway cat. Detective W.L. Johnson of the Criminal Investigation Bureau took most of the calls himself and most of them were prank calls and schoolyard rumour.

One call stood out. A construction worker in the subdivision said someone had phoned him calling himself the Axe Man, complaining about people dumping stumps, limbs and brush on his property and asking him to meet that night to sort it out. Police staked the place out. Nobody turned up.

That phone call is the closest thing to a motive in the whole case, and it points somewhere dull. A local man with a grudge about trespassing and dumping, in a half-built subdivision, using a costume to scare people off his patch.

sections.h: How a man with a hatchet became a murderer
p: In 1973 a University of Maryland student named Patricia Johnson wrote a paper logging exactly 54 versions of the two incidents. The plot held, the details drifted, and a few versions already had the Bunny Man killing people, which the police record never did.

The version everyone repeats now came later. In 1999 somebody posting as Timothy J. Forbes on a site called Castle of Spirits wrote that the Bunny Man was a convict named Douglas J. Grifon who escaped from a bus in 1904 and butchered people at the bridge for decades. Conley checked it line by line and every specific in it is false, including the Old Clifton Library the writer claimed as his source, which never existed.
Two odd nights in 1970, one good newspaper story, and then fifty years of people adding gore because it makes a better campfire story. That's the whole mystery, as far as I can tell.

The Colchester Overpass is a narrow railroad bridge that Colchester Road passes under near Clifton, built around 1906 beside the old Sangster's Station. It's on a working rail line, so the tracks on top are live and the ground around them is not yours.

Because of the legend the bridge became a place to go at night, and it's covered in graffiti from decades of visitors. Fairfax County started controlling access around Halloween back in 2003, and over Halloween in 2011 more than 200 people were turned away at a 14-hour checkpoint, some of them from as far as the Pennsylvania line.

You can drive under it and have a look, and people do every week. What you shouldn't do is climb the embankment or walk the tracks. The real danger there is trains and a trespassing charge. (The costumed-man-in-the-woods part has a cousin in England worth reading about, [Spring-heeled Jack](/creatures/spring-heeled-jack/).)

faq.a: Two incidents are documented. In October 1970 a man in a rabbit outfit threw a hatchet through a car window in Burke, Virginia, and a man in a bunny costume chopped at a porch post and threatened a security guard nearby. Brian Conley, the Fairfax County library historian, found no record of any killing, and the escaped inmate story everyone repeats is a 1999 internet invention.

faq.q: Is the Bunny Man still alive?
faq.a: Nobody knows who he was. If he was the roughly 20-year-old the security guard described in 1970 he'd be in his mid seventies now. There hasn't been a documented attack since, only the story getting bigger.

faq.q: Can you visit Bunny Man Bridge?
faq.a: You can drive under it on Colchester Road near Clifton, Virginia, and that's the sane way to see it. The overpass carries an active railroad line, so don't climb up or walk the tracks. Police watch the area around Halloween and have turned away hundreds of people at checkpoints.

faq.q: Why does the Bunny Man have an axe?
faq.a: Because both 1970 reports describe one. A hatchet came through a car window in the first and a long-handled axe hit a porch post in the second. Later versions turned the axe into something supernatural, but the original was a tool a local man probably kept in his truck.

faq.q: Where did the asylum escape story come from?
faq.a: A 1999 post on a website called Castle of Spirits, written by somebody using the name Timothy J. Forbes. It named the Bunny Man as Douglas J. Grifon, an inmate who escaped in 1904 and killed people at the bridge. Conley found every detail false, including the library the author cited. It never existed.
